text.p: Voters in impoverished Nicaragua may vote with their stomachs in the Oct. 20 presidential poll -- boosting the fortunes of the left-wing Sandinistas, political analysts said on Thursday.
The country's 23 presidential candidates, ranging from communists to capitalists, have almost all made campaign promises to end Nicaragua's brutal poverty and cut high unemployment.

"The problem now is the enormous impoverishment and unemployment suffered by the Nicaraguan people. The Sandinista Front must prepare to attack this disease," current Sandinista candidate and former President Daniel Ortega told reporters.

The right-wing Liberal Alliance, which leads the polls, has made job creation its number one priority, and the Liberal Unity Party has even promised to create 500,000 jobs if elected -- an amazing if unlikely feat in a country of 4.2 million people.

The most recent CID-Gallup poll showed that 77 percent of Nicaraguans thought unemployment was the most important election issue, far outdistancing the issues of crime and corruption that obsess other Latin American countries.

"It's the economy. When all is said and done people vote with their stomachs and right now the people are suffering," the president of CID-Gallup Costa Rica, Carlos Denton, said after the release of the poll.

The country's next president faces a daunting task in taming poverty and unemployment. A recent United Nations study placed Nicaragua as the least developed country in Latin America after Haiti, basing its measurement on per capita income, life expectancy and educational levels.

More than 50 percent of Nicaraguans live in poverty, 75 percent have unsatisfied basic needs and 54 percent of the work-age population is either unemployed or underemployed, according to official figures.
Crowds of children beg at street lights in Managua, Nicaragua's capital, and a doctor in a state hospital makes less than $100 a month.
Nicaraguan economist Mario Arana said the issue of poverty has benefited Sandinista candidate Ortega, who has soared from 20 percent in the polls at the end of 1995 to 35 percent today.
Ortega, who headed Nicaragua's Marxist Sandinista government from 1979 to 1990, is running a close second to Liberal Alliance candidate Arnoldo Aleman ahead of the vote.

Arana said many Nicaraguans felt nostalgic for early years of the Sandinista government when the state supplied food and medical care -- forgetting the latter years when the economy collapsed and store shelves were left empty.
"People have a selective memory," he said.
More than six years after the end of the civil war between the Sandinistas and U.S.-backed Contra rebels and the fall of the Marxist government, Nicaragua has still not put its economy back together.
